tier_reason: bench/bench.txt is first-party poop output comparing hparse with picohttpparser and httparse. The picohttpparser row (1.45s / 6.16G cycles / 34.7G instr) and the hparse row (1.27s / 5.38G / 8.01G, delta -12.5% / -12.6% / -76.9%) match the claim. The benchmark code and flags are public (bench/Makefile, bench/picohttpparser/Makefile, bench/hparse/build.zig), but no CPU model is given for this run, so it stays C. A third-party re-run in PR #2 names a CPU (Ryzen 7 8745HS), but I did not upgrade to A: the baseline is built without ISA flags while hparse targets the native CPU, and no compiler versions are given.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: hparse: zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast (bench/hparse/build.zig uses standardTargetOptions, so the default target is the native CPU). httparse 1.10.0: cargo build --release with [profile.release] opt-level=3 and no target-cpu. picohttpparser: bench/picohttpparser/Makefile runs `gcc ./main.c ./picohttpparser.c -I. -O3` on a vendored copy, with no -msse4.2 or -march flag, not the upstream Makefile. No compiler versions are stated.
corrections.hardware: Unspecified x86-64 (AMD64) Linux machine, according to the maintainer's comment in PR #2. No CPU model is stated for the bench.txt run.
corrections.workload: poop (like hyperfine, but with hardware counters; bench.txt comes from `poop -d 10000`) runs standalone binaries for picohttpparser (C), httparse (Rust) and hparse (Zig). Each binary parses one fixed 430-byte HTTP/1.1 GET request with 9 headers into a 32-slot header array, 10,000,000 times. Metrics: wall time, peak RSS, CPU cycles, instructions retired, cache references and misses, branch misses.
corrections.caveats: 1) No CPU model or compiler versions are given for the bench.txt run (it only says AMD64 Linux, in PR #2), so it is capped at C. 2) The baseline build is not like-for-like. picohttpparser is compiled with plain `gcc -O3` and no -msse4.2 or -march, so its `#ifdef __SSE4_2__` fast path is probably compiled out on a default x86-64 GCC. It retires about 3470 instructions per parse, roughly 8 per byte (derived from page data), which is consistent with the scalar path. hparse is built for the native CPU. 3) The win depends on the platform. On Apple Silicon, hparse is slower than picohttpparser. The maintainer's open issue #3 shows M4 Pro hyperfine times of hparse 1.464s vs picohttpparser 0.965s vs httparse 0.753s, and PR #2 on an M3 shows hparse 2.015s vs picohttpparser 1.252s. 4) A third party reproduced the x86 result in PR #2 on an AMD Ryzen 7 8745HS: hparse 1.01s vs picohttpparser 1.14s wall time (-11.3%), 4.91G vs 5.54G cycles. 5) This is a microbenchmark that repeats one request from a single host. 12.5% less wall time is about 1.14x faster (derived from page data).

notes: The claimed numbers are accurate, but the gain is modest and only shown on x86-64, against a picohttpparser build that probably lacks its SSE4.2 path; hparse is about 1.5x slower than picohttpparser on Apple Silicon (issue #3, still open). Metadata checks out: MIT, 38 stars, not a fork or archived, last commit 2025-10-24 (active). The record said picohttpparser was built via the 'upstream Makefile'; it actually uses a vendored copy with a custom gcc -O3 one-line Makefile, which I corrected.
